title: Himalayan Cedar: Ancient Deodars You Can Visit
meta_description: Not one deodar mapped here grows within three thousand kilometres of the Himalaya. Eighteen of them, in thirteen European cities.
intro: Not one of these eighteen trees grows within three thousand kilometres of the mountains it is named after. Cedrus deodara comes from the western Himalaya, from Afghanistan through to Nepal, where deodar means timber of the gods and a tree can pass a thousand years. It reached Europe in 1822 and the continent's park builders took to it at once: Florence's specimen was on the botanical garden's books by 1880, and Bergamo's stands alone in the middle of a lawn with its own lightning conductor, because it is the tallest thing for some distance. The drooping branch tips are the field mark that separates a deodar from the stiffer cedars of Lebanon and the Atlas. Thirteen cities hold them, most of them Italian, and the two registers that measured the one in Rome disagree about its waist by nearly two metres.
